feedback: If a part is mislabelled, point back to its function: the anther is where pollen is made/held; the stigma is the sticky landing surface for pollen.
If ovules are confused with seeds, clarify that ovules sit inside the ovary and only become seeds after fertilisation.
Reinforce correct location of the carpel parts (stigma → style → ovary → ovules) as a top-to-bottom path.
activities.intendedInsight: A flower's parts are physical structures with specific functions. Examining or handling a real flower (or model) makes those structures concrete, though a clear 2D cross-section can also support labelling; neither is a universal requirement. The goal is to be able to reason later about how each structure affects reproductive success.
learnerActions: Examine a real flower (or a high-fidelity model if a real one is unavailable) and locate each structure by eye and, where possible, by touch.
Find the pollen on the anthers and feel the sticky stigma before any labels are given.
Label the main parts: sepals, petals, stamen (anther + filament), carpel (stigma + style + ovary containing ovules).
Open or drill into the carpel to find the hidden ovules, and name each part's job alongside its name.
activities.title: Dissect and label a real flower

feedback: If a learner says all flowers are bright and scented, point to the dull, scentless, nectarless wind-pollinated flower as a counterexample.
If features are only listed without function, prompt: 'What does this feature DO, and how does that help pollen reach another flower?'

If a learner says bees pollinate on purpose, clarify that pollination is an incidental consequence of insects seeking food (nectar, and for bees also pollen to eat); the flower's structures exploit that behaviour, which is the cause-and-effect point behind the adaptation argument.
Affirm answers phrased as cause→effect arguments tied to reproductive success, not just feature lists.
activities.intendedInsight: Two very different-looking flowers are solving the same problem (getting pollen to another flower) in two ways: one attracts insects with colour and nectar, the other releases clouds of light pollen to the wind. Each feature is an adaptation whose cause→effect link to reproductive success can be argued. Crucially, insects do not set out to pollinate — pollination is an incidental consequence of food-seeking (nectar and/or pollen) that the flower's structures exploit.
learnerActions: Compare side by side an insect-pollinated bloom (bright scented petals, nectar, sticky/spiky pollen) and a wind-pollinated grass flower (small dull flowers, no scent or nectar, feathery stigmas, light abundant pollen).
Build a comparison table: for each feature, state its function and how it raises the chance of pollen reaching another flower.

For each adaptation, answer 'why does this raise the plant's chance of making seeds?' as an explicit cause→effect statement (e.g. 'bright petals cause more insect visits, which raises the chance of pollination').
Explain why an insect visiting a flower ends up transferring pollen to another flower even though it is only seeking food (nectar, or pollen to eat), not trying to pollinate.
activities.title: Two flowers, one problem: wind vs insect pollination

feedback: If a learner says the flower is fertilised the instant pollen lands, separate the two steps: pollination = pollen transfer to the stigma; fertilisation = male and female cells joining in the ovule, which happens later, and only after that does a seed form.
If a learner credits the bee or wind with 'making' the seed, clarify the pollinator only carries pollen; the seed forms from the fertilised ovule inside the flower.
If seed and fruit are conflated, retrace: fertilised ovule → seed, ovary → fruit.

Reasoning check: 'If we bagged a flower so no insects could reach it but shook its own pollen onto its stigma, could it still make seeds?' As a thought experiment the answer is yes — pollination can still occur (self-pollination) and fertilisation can follow — which shows the two steps are separate and that insects are not what makes the seed. Note that some species are self-incompatible, so real self-pollination does not always produce seeds; treat this as a test of the pollination/fertilisation distinction rather than a universal guarantee.
activities.intendedInsight: Making a seed is a sequence of distinct steps, not a single moment. Pollination and fertilisation are separate events, and seed and fruit develop from different structures and serve a different purpose from dispersal.
learnerActions: Sequence the stages: pollen lands on stigma → pollen tube grows down the style → fertilises the ovule → ovule becomes seed, ovary becomes fruit → seed is dispersed.

State in your own words how pollination differs from fertilisation: pollination is the TRANSFER of pollen from anther to stigma; fertilisation is the later fusion of gamete nuclei after the pollen tube grows down.

Identify which part becomes the seed (the fertilised ovule) and which becomes the fruit (the ovary around it), and what the petals do in insect-pollinated flowers (attract pollinators, then usually wither and fall away).

Explain how pollination and dispersal serve different purposes: pollination delivers pollen (which carries the male gametes) to the stigma so that fertilisation can follow; dispersal spreads offspring away from the parent to reduce competition and reach new places to grow.
activities.title: Trace the journey: pollination to dispersal

feedback: If a learner states a conclusion without data, prompt them to point to the measurements or plot that support it.
If only mechanisms are listed without being explained, ask how the structure causes the seed to travel away from the parent.

Encourage controlling the drop height, paper type, added mass, release method and any airflow, and repeating measurements, so that wing size is the only thing that changes and comparisons between wing sizes are fair.
activities.intendedInsight: Dispersal adaptations can be investigated empirically: measured data about wing size and fall-time/distance support an evidence-based argument about which structures disperse seeds most effectively.
learnerActions: Build winged 'helicopter' paper seeds of varying wing size.

Drop them from a fixed height and measure fall-time for each design (longer fall-time means more time for wind to carry the seed). If measuring dispersal distance, use a steady sideways airflow (e.g. a fan on a fixed setting at a fixed position), because a drop in still air gives little sideways travel. Keep the paper type and any added mass (e.g. one paper clip) the same so that only wing size changes, and repeat each drop.

Record the data (using means of repeats), plot fall-time or distance against wing area, and argue from the plot which wing design is likely to disperse best and why, noting that fall-time stands in for how far wind could carry the seed and that the trend may not keep rising for very large wings.
Describe at least two dispersal mechanisms from the wider set (winged/wind, hooked or edible/animal, explosive, water) and explain how each works.
activities.title: Quantitative dispersal investigation

feedback: If a claim is asserted without support, ask what observation or measurement backs it.
If reasoning stops at a feature, push for the causal link to reproductive success.
Best used after dispersal data has been collected, so arguments can draw on real evidence.
activities.intendedInsight: Scientific claims about adaptations must be backed by evidence and reasoning; practising the back-and-forth of justification can strengthen the argument-from-evidence skill.
learnerActions: Take the role of a botanist and justify a pollination or dispersal claim when probed (e.g. 'What evidence shows bright petals raise reproductive success?').
Respond to follow-up challenges by citing specific adaptations or measured data (ideally the dispersal data you collected).
Construct a short spoken or written argument linking a structure to its effect on reproductive success.
activities.title: Defend your claim: botanist argument
